header: Date: 2026-08-05, Start: 16:00 UTC, Duration: 62 minutes. Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Carlos Ruiz (Redwood SE), Markus Varela (Aurelia Head of AI), Lina Chen (Aurelia Platform Eng), Samir Patel (Aurelia Infosec). Recording link: (internal)
summary: Workshop to finalize POC acceptance gates, go/no-go thresholds, and the reporting artifact format. Focus areas: latency/throughput SLOs, quality pass rates on representative prompts, workload sizing for dedicated vs hosted, security evidence needed for acceptance. Agreed to use a standard CSV + JSON summary bundle plus raw logs and a short runbook video for signoff.
topics: Workload sizing: sustained QPS and burst handling
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for carving time. Quick roll call?
[00:08] Markus: Markus here. Lina, Samir — yes.
[00:12] Lina: hi all, Lina.
[00:15] Jordan: Great. Agenda — finish the acceptance gates and the actual report we hand to your steering committee. We want a concrete go/no-go rubric.
[00:28] Priya: I'll jump into the measurement pieces. We built a benchmark template that captures per-prompt latency distribution, top-1 quality, hallucination flag rate, and cost per 1k tokens.
[00:40] Markus: Important for us: clinical recall on our triage prompts must not drop more than 1.5 points vs baseline model. Also we need p95 latency under 300 ms for synchronous flows, ideally <200 ms but we can talk tradeoffs.
[00:55] Samir: Security — we need audit logs, SSO flows, and proof of data-in-transit encryption. For private deployment, KMS integration and separation of telemetry is a must.
[01:08] Carlos: Noted, we'll include the security checklist in the delivery artifacts. For the SLOs, can you confirm what sustained load looks like?
[01:15] Lina: Our baseline is roughly 180 qps sustained with 800ms average payload, bursts up to 600 qps during clinic hours.
[01:24] Priya: Ok, so for POC we should size for 200 qps sustained and validate burst handling to 600 with graceful degradation. We'll include a cold-start/scale-up test.
[01:34] Markus: What about cost gating? We need a unit economics boundary — if the cost to serve goes above X per 1k tokens, we have to consider dedicated or quantized variants.
[01:45] Jordan: We're proposing a cost threshold of $0.65 per 1k tokens for the POC as a go/no-go — that's adjustable. If average cost is higher, we recommend model quantization or pinning a cheaper variant for most traffic.
[01:58] Lina: We also need quality pass criteria. For our sample set of 3k labeled prompts: at least 92% correct/acceptable outputs and <3% hallucination flags. How do you normally measure hallucination?
[02:12] Priya: We include human-labeled spot checks plus an automated scoring column in the CSV. The template has columns: prompt_id, prompt_text, expected_label, model_output, automated_score, human_score, hallucination_flag, latency_ms, tokens_in, tokens_out, cost_usd.
[02:28] Markus: That CSV layout is good. Can you include a field for inference_variant so we can track which model or quantization was used?
[02:37] Carlos: Yes, inference_variant will be a required column. We'll also ask teams to attach raw traces for any failure cases.
[02:45] Samir: On telemetry — we need logs for 30 days and an audit trail for config changes during the POC. Is that doable for Hosted?
[02:53] Jordan: For Hosted we can provide logs and retention for the POC window; for Private we give you full control. We'll call out exactly which logs we can export.
[03:02] Lina: One more on metrics: include p50/p90/p95/p99 and tail-latency count. If p99 is > 1.5 seconds that's a red flag for us.
[03:12] Priya: Agreed. For acceptance we recommend: p95 <= 300 ms (soft), p95 <= 220 ms (preferred), p99 <= 1500 ms (hard stop). Throughput: sustain 200 qps for 30 minutes with <5% error rate. Quality: pass-rate >= 92% on labeled set; hallucination <3%. Cost: average <= $0.65 per 1k tokens.
[03:35] Markus: Those thresholds look reasonable. For the go/no-go decision, who signs off on the quality gate?
[03:40] Jordan: We typically require the customer product owner plus the vendor SE to sign the acceptance packet. We'll include a checklist to collect signatures.
[03:48] Lina: What does the acceptance packet look like?
[03:52] Carlos: Template: 1) CSV of per-prompt metrics; 2) JSON summary with aggregated stats; 3) raw server logs (zipped); 4) short recorded demo showing typical flow + a runbook video of the benchmark run; 5) security evidence (SSO audit, KMS cert scan).
[04:11] Samir: For security evidence, we need an exportable artifact stating which keys were used, proof of encryption, and confirmation we don't persist PHI.
[04:22] Jordan: We'll provide a security pack with pointers to SOC 2 artifacts and a letter describing data handling. For Private deployments we can provide more granular KMS notes.
[04:31] Markus: Timeline—what do you need from us to start runs?
[04:35] Priya: Representative prompt sets (3 sets: triage, patient-info summarization, clinician suggestions), and expected labels. Also an infra contact and dev account to push ephemeral agents.
[04:45] Lina: I'll send those by Aug 10. Is two weeks enough to run full benchmark?
[04:49] Carlos: Two weeks is tight but doable if the datasets are ready. We'll run warm-up, steady-state, burst tests, and the quality annotation pass. Final report in five business days after runs.
[04:59] Markus: So schedule wise: get data Aug 10, run Aug 11–19, report Aug 24?
[05:06] Jordan: Sounds workable. We'll aim for Aug 24 for the acceptance packet, so your steering committee can review on Aug 26.
[05:12] Lina: On the benchmark runbook — can you include the exact load generator script and the seeds so we can reproduce?
[05:18] Priya: Yes, we'll include the Taurus/Locust scripts and the exact flags. Also instructions for priming KV cache and prefix caching, because that affects latency numbers.
[05:27] Markus: On priming — we need to see both cold and primed numbers. For acceptance we want a primed run to meet the threshold, but also documentation of cold-start behavior.
[05:36] Jordan: We'll deliver both. For priming we recommend pre-warming the KV cache with a 20-minute synthetic run, that's in the template.
[05:44] Samir: A quick note: include a section that lists what would cause an automatic fail — e.g., breaches in data handling, unexplained spike in error rate >10%, p99 > 3s for majority of requests.
[05:56] Carlos: We'll add a fail-criteria appendix.
[06:00] Markus: Can we have a sample acceptance CSV populated with synthetic examples so our reviewers can see the fields?
[06:06] Jordan: Absolutely, we'll send a populated sample with anonymized entries.
[06:11] Lina: Regarding deployment — if hosted fails the cost gate, can Redwood spin up a dedicated pool just for us during POC?
[06:18] Jordan: We can recommend Dedicated for predictable throughput; depending on timing we can provision a small reserved pool or use burst capacity. We'll note the lead time.
[06:26] Priya: For the report format: primary artifact is CSV, secondary is aggregated JSON with p50/p90/p95/p99 and pass/fail booleans per gate, plus a human review sheet. The email subject line should follow the template: "POC Acceptance Packet — Aurelia — YYYYMMDD".
[06:45] Markus: Ok. Last thing: who on Redwood will be our point of contact during the runs?
[06:49] Jordan: Primary is Priya for infra/benchmarking, Jordan for commercial and signoff, Carlos for troubleshooting.
[06:56] Lina: Great. Thanks all.
[06:59] Jordan: Recap — Jordan to send benchmark template + sample CSV by Aug 7; Lina to provide datasets by Aug 10; Redwood runs Aug 11–19; report Aug 24. Security attachments will be provided in the acceptance packet. Any other blockers?
[07:12] Samir: No blockers, just we will review the security pack as early as possible.
[07:18] Jordan: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up in email and book the infra kickoff.
[07:24] [call ends]
